name: Afghanistan
sources: READ THIS FIRST. Afghanistan is the one nation in this roster for which the World Bank series the rest of it is built on DOES NOT EXIST. NY.GDP.MKTP.CD returns null for AFG for 1990 and for every year until 2002; there is no World Bank national-accounts observation for Afghanistan at this date, because there was no functioning statistical office in a country eleven years into a civil war. Every economic figure below therefore comes from a different source or is explicitly a judgement, and each says which it is. This file is the honest gap in this region's submission, not a confident reconstruction.

GDP $3.0bn: CIA World Factbook 1990, Afghanistan entry, verbatim — 'GDP: $3 billion, per capita $200; real growth rate 0% (1989 est.)'. This is a 1989 estimate carried to the 1990 start, and the same Factbook entry warns in its own words that government claims notwithstanding, gross domestic product almost certainly was lower than ten years earlier because of the loss of labour and capital and the disruption of trade and transport. Entered as published.

Population 12.0m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series AFG, 1990 = 12,045,660. THIS DISAGREES WITH THE SOURCE THE GDP CAME FROM AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS THE POINT. The CIA World Factbook 1990 gives 'Population: 15,862,293 (July 1990), growth rate 7.7% (1990)'. The gap of about 3.8m is the refugees — roughly five to six million Afghans were in Pakistan and Iran in 1990, and the absurd 7.7% growth rate in the Factbook line is not births, it is the beginning of their return. The World Bank figure counts residents; the CIA figure counts Afghans. The resident figure is entered because it is the population the economy and the army actually drew on in January 1990. The consequence is stated rather than hidden: $3.0bn over 12.0m is $250 per head, where the Factbook's own pairing gives $200. Neither number is reconciled here, because reconciling them would mean inventing one.

TFP trend 0.002: the floor of this roster's range, and the only defensible value for an economy whose source says its real growth rate was zero and its output was below where it had been a decade earlier. Irrigation systems were destroyed, roughly a third of the population had left, and the modern sector existed only where Soviet advisers were standing.

Inflation 50%: CIA World Factbook 1990, Afghanistan entry, verbatim — 'Inflation rate (consumer prices): over 50% (1989 est.)'. 'Over 50%' is transcribed as 50%, which is the floor the phrase permits and therefore the least invented reading of it. The true figure was higher and unmeasured.

Interest rate 20%: THIS IS THE ONE FIGURE IN THIS FILE THAT IS NOT TRANSCRIBED FROM ANY SOURCE, AND IT IS SAID PLAINLY. Da Afghanistan Bank did not operate a market policy rate; the banking system was a state disbursement channel for Soviet subsidy and no policy rate for 1990 is published anywhere I could reach. A number is nevertheless required by the schema. 20% is placed so that the real-rate gap it implies, 0.025 - (0.20 - 0.50) = 0.325, is exactly Yugoslavia's — the widest gap the shipped roster reaches and its stated honest extreme. That is a modelling decision made in the open: it says 'this economy had deeply negative real rates, as far negative as anything else on this board, and no more precision than that is available'. It is listed as unverified in this region's report.

Revenue 9% of GDP: A JUDGEMENT, NOT A MEASUREMENT. The CIA World Factbook 1990 gives 'Budget: revenues NA; expenditures $646.7 million, including capital expenditures of $370.2 million (FY87 est.)' — the revenue line is literally NA in the source. Expenditure of $646.7m against a $3bn economy is 21.6% of GDP, and the gap between that and what Kabul could collect was Soviet transfers, running at billions of dollars a year. 9% is entered as the collection side, level with Bangladesh's and above Nigeria's 8%, on the reasoning that a government holding the cities and not the countryside taxes about as well as the weakest peacetime states in this roster.

Military 15% of GDP and a strength index of 8: NEITHER IS A PUBLISHED SERIES. World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS returns null for AFG for 1990 and the Factbook entry carries no defence expenditure line. The DRA fielded roughly 100,000 men in the armed forces plus a comparable body of tribal and regional militias, and had been given a very large stock of Soviet equipment — Scud batteries fired in defence of Jalalabad, MiG-23s, several hundred tanks. 15% of GDP is set below Iraq's 0.20, this roster's ceiling and a state that had just finished an eight-year war, and far above Israel's 0.124: Afghanistan was spending more than any of them in the sense that mattered, but most of it was somebody else's money and does not sit inside its own GDP. Strength 8 is indexed above Myanmar's 6 for the equipment and below Pakistan's 16, and deliberately not higher, because the striking fact about the DRA army was how much of it defected: Shahnawaz Tanai, the defence minister, attempted a coup with air force support on 6 March 1990 and fled to Peshawar.

Public investment 5% and private investment 3% of GDP: A JUDGEMENT. No capital formation series exists for Afghanistan in 1990. What is stated is the shape rather than the magnitude — a war economy in which almost the only capital being formed was state capital financed by Moscow, and in which private investment had very nearly stopped because there was no property anyone expected to keep.

Debt 60% of GDP: CIA World Factbook 1990 — 'External debt: $1.8 billion (December 1989 est.)' — against the same source's $3.0bn GDP, which gives 0.60. Both halves of this ratio come from the same entry in the same source, which makes it the most internally consistent figure in the file. Same stated substitution as the rest of this region: the schema field means gross public debt and this is external debt.

Oil 0.0 mbd: Afghanistan produced no meaningful crude. Its hydrocarbon was natural gas from the Sheberghan fields in Jowzjan, piped north to the Soviet Union under an arrangement in which the meters were on the Soviet side — a long-standing Afghan grievance and not a crude output this field can carry.

Stability 25 and authoritarianism 0.85: the lowest stability in this roster, below Nigeria's 35, and the justification is that this regime had twenty-six months left. Mohammad Najibullah's government held Kabul, Jalalabad, Herat and the ring road and very little else; it had repelled the mujahideen assault on Jalalabad in 1989, survived the Tanai coup attempt in March 1990, and collapsed in April 1992 within months of the Soviet aid that sustained it ending with the Soviet Union itself. That is the single most important dependency in this nation's entry and the model should be allowed to find it. Authoritarianism 0.85 is set level with the USSR, Iran and Saudi Arabia and below Vietnam's 0.92: the 1987 constitution and the National Reconciliation policy had formally ended the one-party state and permitted satellite parties, and there was a National Assembly elected in April 1988, but the PDPA held every institution that mattered and the security service ran the country.

Separatism 0.20: set deliberately BELOW Turkey's 0.30, which is counter-intuitive for a country in the eleventh year of a civil war, and the reason is what this field measures. Separatism here is nationalities strain — the pull of a region to leave the state. Afghanistan's war was not a secession. The mujahideen parties were regionally and ethnically based and fought each other along those lines, but not one of them proposed to detach a province; every faction was fighting for Kabul, which is the opposite of separatism and is why the country stayed within its borders through everything that followed. 0.20 records the ethnic fracture of the resistance without pretending it was an independence movement.
